query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloy protective coatings, the incorporation of reactive dopants (such as Y and Hf) enhances the formation and stability of a continuous, adherent oxide layer during high-temperature frictional wear. This oxide layer mediates the wear process by reducing metal-to-metal contact and minimizing adhesive wear, thereby improving overall wear resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: An AlCoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloy coating prepared by laser cladding without Y/Hf dopants.
generation.intervention: Introduce controlled amounts of Y and Hf into the HEA coating formulation.
generation.conditions: High-temperature frictional wear tests (e.g., at or near 900°C) under conditions relevant to harsh service environments (such as those including molten salt environments or high load sliding friction).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a thin, adherent, protective oxide scale (possibly enriched in the doped reactive elements) on the coating’s surface.
generation.mechanism: Y and Hf have a high oxygen affinity and promote the nucleation and growth of a stable oxide film during wear. This film acts as a barrier that limits direct metal-to-metal contact and reduces the severity of adhesive and abrasive wear modes, effectively transforming the wear mechanism into one where oxidative processes, which are less damaging, predominate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped baseline coating, the Y/Hf-doped coating will exhibit a lower wear rate (i.e., reduced wear scar depth/volume loss) and a lower friction coefficient. Microscopically, it will show a more continuous and adherent oxide layer under the tested high-temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: The HEA coating without Y/Hf doping, which typically exhibits a mix of adhesive, abrasive, and oxidation wear under high-temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic effect is expected to hold under high-temperature applications (approximately ≥800°C) and under friction conditions where oxidation can occur. Outside these temperature or environmental ranges, the effect of the dopants on the oxide formation may be less pronounced.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies support that doping with reactive elements can stabilize oxide layers at high temperatures, the precise quantitative improvement in wear resistance (i.e., percentage decrease in wear rate) and the dopant concentration needed for optimal oxide formation remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings via laser cladding: one set doped with Y and Hf (YHf-HEA) and one undoped baseline sample. Subject both sets to high-temperature (around 900°C) frictional wear tests under identical mechanical loads and corrosive environmental conditions. Perform SEM and EDS analyses on the wear tracks to evaluate the presence and continuity of oxide layers.
measurements: Wear rate (measured as scar depth and volume loss)
Oxide layer thickness and continuity (via SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y/Hf-doped coatings do not show a statistically significant reduction in wear rate or friction coefficient, and if there is no evidence of a well-formed, continuous, protective oxide layer compared to the undoped baseline, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Therefore, in order to investigate the high-temperature protective capabilities of EHEA coatings, AlCoCrFeNi2.1 and AlCoCrFeNi2.1 co-doping with Y and Hf (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding in this paper. After their preparation, the microstructure and high-temperature thermal stability of the coatings were characterized, and the hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% (wt.%) NaCl mixed molten salt was investigated, which provided data support for an evaluation of the potential applications of high-entropy alloy coatings in harsh service environments such as steam pipelines and the hot-end components of gas turbines.

cited_evidence.text: From the EDS, it can be seen that the O content on the surface is higher than that in the other samples, which indicates that this sample has experienced more severe oxidative wear during the frictional wear process. Combined with the above analysis, it can be seen that the alloy has a wear mechanism of abrasive wear, adhesive wear and oxidation wear in the process of friction and wear.
